triage.name: Head Injuries
triage.reason: Traumatic brain injury with altered mental status; diagnosis reachable by history, exam and imaging, with critical severity stratification.

demographics: More common in males, especially in adolescents and young adults
Falls are the leading cause in older adults and young children
Motor vehicle crashes and sports injuries predominate in adolescents and young adults

risk_factors.text: Recent fall, especially from a height or in an older adult

social_history: Occupational exposure to falls or blunt trauma

chief_complaints.text: I blacked out for a moment

hpi.onset: Sudden, immediately after a blow to the head, fall, crash or collision
hpi.duration: Minutes to hours at presentation; symptoms can persist for days to weeks after a concussion
hpi.progression: Headache and confusion are worst in the first minutes to hours; nausea, dizziness and memory trouble may build over the first day. Worsening headache, repeated vomiting, drowsiness or new weakness suggests an expanding intracranial injury and needs urgent evaluation.
hpi.location: Diffuse head pain, often worst at the site of impact; neck pain if there was a whiplash component
hpi.radiation: Usually none; neck pain may radiate to the shoulders
hpi.quality: Aching, pressure-like or throbbing head pain; the injury itself is described as a blow or impact
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate in most patients; severe and worsening in those with intracranial bleeding
hpi.timing: Constant after the injury, often worse with movement, bending or straining
relieving: Resting in a quiet, dark room
Ice at the site of impact

associated_symptoms.text: Trouble remembering the injury or the moments around it
Trouble concentrating or feeling slowed down
Sleeping more or less than usual
Clear fluid or blood from the nose or ear
A seizure right after the injury

pertinent_negatives: No fever or neck stiffness before the injury
No sudden worst headache of life without trauma
No focal weakness or numbness before the injury
No speech difficulty before the injury
No recent illness with rash, joint pain or weight loss
No known bleeding disorder or anticoagulant use (if applicable)

positives.text: Feeling warm or sweaty after the event
Memory trouble around the time of injury
Numbness or weakness in an arm or leg

negatives: Loss of consciousness lasting more than a few minutes
One pupil larger than the other
argues_against: Stroke or seizure disorder without trauma

positives.text: Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ear

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants and young children may present with irritability, poor feeding, vomiting or a bulging fontanelle rather than reporting headache or confusion. Non-accidental trauma should be considered when the mechanism does not fit the injury.
missing_classic_features: Clear description of loss of consciousness

atypical.how_it_differs: Even a minor fall can cause a subdural hematoma, and symptoms may be subtle: new confusion, gait change or drowsiness rather than a dramatic headache. Anticoagulant use raises the risk substantially.

Trauma evaluation must also consider the pregnancy; imaging decisions balance fetal radiation exposure against the need to exclude intracranial bleeding. Symptoms of head injury can be confused with preeclampsia or eclampsia.
A minor head injury can be more serious because of bleeding risk from low platelets or coagulopathy; infection of a scalp wound or skull fracture is also more likely.

general.mild: Alert, awake, conversant; may look dazed or hold the head; no external signs of serious injury
general.moderate: Drowsy but arousable, disoriented to time or place, may vomit or need help sitting up
general.severe: Difficult to arouse, confused or combative, obvious scalp or facial trauma, may have focal deficits
general.critical: Unresponsive or only to painful stimuli, abnormal posturing, dilated or asymmetric pupils, hemodynamic instability

findings.maneuver: Assess eye opening, verbal response and motor response to voice and painful stimulus
findings.finding: Glasgow Coma Scale score below 15; mild 13–15, moderate 9–12, severe 3–8

findings.maneuver: Shine a light in each eye and compare pupil size and reactivity
findings.finding: One pupil larger than the other or sluggish to react, suggesting uncal herniation or third nerve compression

findings.maneuver: Test strength in all four limbs and compare sides
findings.finding: Weakness or drift of one arm or leg

findings.maneuver: Stroke the sole of each foot from heel to toe
findings.finding: Upgoing toe (extensor plantar response) on one or both sides

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient their name, where they are, the date and what happened
findings.finding: Disorientation, confusion, slowed responses or inability to recall the injury

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the entire scalp, parting the hair
findings.finding: Laceration, abrasion, contusion or boggy swelling at the site of impact

findings.maneuver: Palpate the skull gently for a step-off or depression
findings.finding: A palpable depression or step-off in the skull contour
Periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes), suggesting a basilar skull fracture
Ecchymosis over the mastoid process (Battle sign), suggesting a basilar skull fracture

findings.maneuver: Inspect the tympanic membranes with an otoscope
findings.finding: Blood behind the eardrum, suggesting a basilar skull fracture

findings.maneuver: Inspect the nose and ears for clear fluid; ask the patient to lean forward
findings.finding: Clear fluid dripping from the nose or ear, suggesting a CSF leak from a basilar skull fracture

findings.maneuver: Palpate the posterior midline of the neck and ask about pain with movement
findings.finding: Midline cervical tenderness or pain on neck movement, raising concern for a cervical spine injury

findings.maneuver: Palpate the midline neck and test active rotation if the patient is alert and has no distracting injury
findings.finding: No midline tenderness and full painless range of motion

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for tenderness, guarding or distension
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender abdomen without guarding

findings.maneuver: Auscultate breath sounds and palpate the chest wall
findings.finding: Clear breath sounds and no chest wall tenderness or crepitus

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the arms and legs for deformity, tenderness or swelling
findings.finding: No deformity, focal tenderness or swelling

labs.caveat: Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before CT imaging; a positive result changes imaging choice and management.
Prolonged in warfarin use, liver disease or disseminated intravascular coagulation; a bleeding risk marker before neurosurgery.
An elevated INR in a patient on warfarin predicts progression of intracranial hemorrhage and guides reversal.
Prolonged with heparin use or a coagulopathy.
Thrombocytopenia raises bleeding risk and may reflect alcohol use, liver disease or a primary hematologic disorder.
Mild leukocytosis is common after trauma and does not by itself indicate infection.
Hyponatremia can follow traumatic brain injury from SIADH or cerebral salt wasting and can worsen confusion or seizures.
Hypoglycemia is a reversible cause of altered mental status and must be excluded in any patient with a head injury and confusion.
Elevated with shock or associated multisystem trauma; supports the need for resuscitation.
Rises after prolonged immobility, seizures or associated muscle trauma; very high values raise concern for rhabdomyolysis.
Only measured if a lumbar puncture is performed; elevated opening pressure suggests raised intracranial pressure.
Blood in the CSF can reflect subarachnoid hemorrhage or a traumatic tap; a lumbar puncture is generally avoided when intracranial bleeding is suspected.
Elevated with subarachnoid blood or central nervous system inflammation.

findings.finding: Sinus bradycardia or relative bradycardia from raised intracranial pressure (Cushing response)
Diffuse deep T-wave inversions with a long QT interval (cerebral T waves), sometimes with prominent U waves
Prolonged QT interval
Sinus tachycardia from pain, stress or associated trauma

imaging.preferred_when: First-line in moderate to severe head injury, any focal deficit, anticoagulant use or concerning mechanism

findings.text: Hyperdense extra-axial collection along the cerebral convexity (acute subdural hematoma)
Hyperdense material in the sulci, cisterns or Sylvian fissure (subarachnoid hemorrhage)
Punctate hyperdense foci in white matter or gray-white junction (diffuse axonal injury)
Hypodense or mixed-density intraparenchymal contusion, often frontal or temporal
Linear lucency through the skull vault (skull fracture)
Midline shift, effaced cisterns or sulcal effacement (mass effect)
Depressed skull fracture fragment below the inner table

imaging.preferred_when: Midline neck tenderness, distracting injury, altered mental status or high-risk mechanism

findings.text: Vertebral body or posterior element fracture

imaging.preferred_when: Persistent neurologic deficits, suspected diffuse axonal injury or symptoms out of proportion to CT findings

findings.text: Multiple small susceptibility artifacts in white matter or gray-white junction (diffuse axonal injury)
Subtle cortical contusions or brainstem lesions not seen on CT
Subacute or chronic subdural hematoma with signal characteristics of blood breakdown products
Usually not performed; CT is the study of choice for suspected skull fracture

initial.why: First-line imaging to exclude intracranial hemorrhage, contusion, mass effect or skull fracture
Reversible cause of altered mental status; must be checked in any confused patient
Baseline hemoglobin and platelet count; screens for anemia and thrombocytopenia
Baseline coagulation status, especially in patients on anticoagulants or with liver disease
Sodium, glucose and renal function; hyponatremia can worsen confusion
Required in anyone who could be pregnant before CT imaging
Clears the cervical spine in patients with midline tenderness, distracting injury or altered mental status
initial.only_if: midline neck tenderness, distracting injury, altered mental status or high-risk mechanism

initial.why: Prepares for possible transfusion or neurosurgery
initial.only_if: severe injury, anemia or planned operative intervention

supporting.why: Assesses perfusion in associated multisystem trauma
Screens for rhabdomyolysis after prolonged immobility, seizures or crush injury
Detects diffuse axonal injury or subtle lesions when symptoms exceed CT findings
supporting.only_if: persistent deficits or symptoms out of proportion to CT

supporting.why: Assesses bleeding risk and guides reversal in patients on warfarin
Assesses bleeding risk and guides reversal in patients on warfarin
Assesses bleeding risk in patients on heparin or with a coagulopathy
Thrombocytopenia raises bleeding risk and may require platelet transfusion before neurosurgery

not_indicated.why: CT is more sensitive and is the standard for suspected skull fracture
Contraindicated when raised intracranial pressure or intracranial mass effect is suspected; risks herniation
No role in the evaluation of head trauma
Not indicated unless abdominal pain or pancreatic injury is suspected
Not part of the acute trauma workup
Not routinely indicated unless urinary tract injury or infection is suspected

decision_points: Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant
Glasgow Coma Scale 8 or less: secure the airway before imaging
Anticoagulated or antiplatelet-treated patients: low threshold for CT and repeat imaging
Cervical spine imaging before clearing the neck in patients with midline tenderness or distracting injury
Signs of herniation or rapidly declining mental status: treat for raised intracranial pressure and involve neurosurgery before or during imaging

criteria.name: Canadian CT Head Rule
criteria.summary: Applies to adults with minor head injury and a Glasgow Coma Scale of 13 to 15. CT is recommended if any high-risk feature is present (failure to reach GCS 15 within 2 hours, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, vomiting, age 65 or older, or signs of basilar skull fracture) or any medium-risk feature is present (amnesia before impact longer than 30 minutes, or a dangerous mechanism such as a pedestrian struck, ejection from a vehicle, or a fall from more than 3 feet or 5 stairs).
items: GCS less than 15 at 2 hours after injury
Suspected open or depressed skull fracture
Amnesia before impact longer than 30 minutes

criteria.name: New Orleans Criteria
criteria.summary: Applies to patients with minor head injury and a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15. CT is recommended if any of the listed features is present.
items: Physical evidence of trauma above the clavicles

criteria.name: PECARN
criteria.summary: Applies to children under 2 years and children 2 years and older with minor head injury. CT is recommended for children with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 14 or less, altered mental status, or signs of skull fracture; imaging is also considered when the mechanism is severe or when vomiting, severe headache or loss of consciousness is present.

differential.name: Acute alcohol or drug intoxication
differential.why_considered: Altered mental status, slurred speech, ataxia and a fall are common in patients who have been drinking, and the trauma may be the reason they fell rather than the result of the fall.
differential.trigger: Alcohol on the breath, slurred speech or ataxia with a reported fall

history: No clear head impact or a low-energy fall
exam: Diffuse neurologic depression without focal deficit
Symptoms improve with time and observation
labs: Negative or low urine drug screen for other agents
imaging: CT head without acute intracranial injury

differential.name: Ischemic stroke
differential.why_considered: Sudden focal weakness, numbness, slurred speech or confusion can be mistaken for a head injury, especially when the patient fell after the neurologic event began.
differential.trigger: Focal deficit that does not fit the reported trauma or that was present before the fall

history: Abrupt onset of focal symptoms before the fall
Vascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes or atrial fibrillation
exam: Focal cortical signs such as aphasia or neglect
No external signs of head trauma
labs: Glucose and coagulation studies to exclude mimics and guide thrombolysis
imaging: CT head without hemorrhage, with early ischemic changes or a hyperdense vessel
MRI with restricted diffusion in a vascular territory

differential.name: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
differential.why_considered: Sudden severe headache, vomiting, neck stiffness and photophobia overlap with head injury, and a ruptured aneurysm can cause a fall with secondary head trauma.
differential.trigger: Worst headache of life with neck stiffness and no clear trauma, or a headache that started before the fall

labs: Xanthochromia or elevated red blood cell count in cerebrospinal fluid if lumbar puncture is performed
imaging: Hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns, sulci or Sylvian fissure on noncontrast CT
Aneurysm on CT angiography or catheter angiography

differential.name: Meningitis or encephalitis
differential.why_considered: Fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and altered mental status can resemble post-traumatic symptoms, and a patient with infection may fall and strike the head.
differential.trigger: Fever, neck stiffness or rash with headache and confusion

history: Fever and systemic illness before the neurologic symptoms
labs: Cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis, elevated protein and low glucose
imaging: CT head without acute traumatic findings
MRI showing meningeal enhancement or temporal lobe signal change in encephalitis

differential.name: Post-traumatic seizure or epilepsy
differential.why_considered: A seizure can cause a fall and head impact, and a head injury can cause a seizure, so the two are easily confused.

history: Witnessed tonic-clonic activity, tongue biting or incontinence
Postictal confusion out of proportion to the injury
Prior seizure history or missed anticonvulsant doses
exam: Postictal drowsiness that improves over minutes to hours
labs: Elevated creatine kinase after a generalized seizure
imaging: CT head to exclude acute traumatic bleeding
MRI to look for a structural cause of seizures

differential.name: Cervical spine injury
differential.why_considered: Neck pain, midline tenderness and neurologic deficits often accompany head trauma and can be missed if attention is focused on the head.
differential.trigger: Midline neck tenderness, distracting injury or a high-risk mechanism

history: High-risk mechanism such as a dive, fall from height or motor vehicle crash
Numbness or weakness in the arms or legs
exam: Sensory level or focal motor deficit
imaging: CT cervical spine showing fracture, subluxation or prevertebral swelling
MRI for ligamentous or spinal cord injury when CT is negative but symptoms persist

differential.name: Metabolic or toxic encephalopathy
differential.why_considered: Hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hepatic encephalopathy, uremia or drug toxicity can cause confusion, dizziness and falls that are attributed to a head injury.

history: Diabetes, liver disease, kidney disease or new medications
exam: Diffuse cognitive impairment without focal deficit
labs: Elevated ammonia, urea or drug levels
imaging: CT head without acute traumatic findings

differential.name: Psychiatric or functional disorder
differential.why_considered: Symptoms such as dizziness, memory trouble, weakness or unresponsiveness can occur without structural injury, and a minor head injury may be the trigger.

history: Prior psychiatric history or psychosocial stressors
exam: Normal reflexes and no focal cortical signs
imaging: Normal CT and MRI of the brain

severity.mild: Glasgow Coma Scale 13–15, alert and conversant, headache and dizziness only, no focal deficit, no vomiting, no anticoagulant use, and a low-risk mechanism; may be managed with observation and return precautions.
severity.moderate: Glasgow Coma Scale 9–12, drowsy but arousable, disoriented, repeated vomiting, focal deficit, post-traumatic seizure, or a skull fracture on imaging; requires admission, close neurologic monitoring and neurosurgical consultation.
severity.severe: Glasgow Coma Scale 3–8, unable to protect the airway, signs of raised intracranial pressure or herniation, or a large intracranial hematoma with mass effect; requires intubation, intensive care and possible surgery.
severity.critical: Unresponsive with abnormal posturing, asymmetric or fixed dilated pupils, hemodynamic instability or a rapidly expanding intracranial hemorrhage; requires immediate airway control, hyperosmolar therapy, blood pressure support and emergency neurosurgery.

red_flags.finding: Glasgow Coma Scale 8 or less or inability to protect the airway
red_flags.meaning: Severe traumatic brain injury; intubate and involve neurosurgery immediately

red_flags.finding: One pupil larger than the other or sluggish to react
red_flags.meaning: Uncal herniation or third nerve compression; a neurosurgical emergency

red_flags.finding: New focal weakness, numbness or slurred speech
red_flags.meaning: Intracranial hemorrhage, contusion or mass effect until proven otherwise

red_flags.finding: Worsening headache, repeated vomiting or increasing drowsiness
red_flags.meaning: Expanding intracranial hematoma or rising intracranial pressure
Cortical irritation from contusion, hemorrhage or fracture; needs imaging and monitoring

red_flags.finding: Clear fluid or blood from the nose or ear, raccoon eyes or Battle sign
red_flags.meaning: Basilar skull fracture with risk of cerebrospinal fluid leak and meningitis

red_flags.finding: Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use with any head impact
red_flags.meaning: High risk of delayed intracranial hemorrhage; low threshold for CT and repeat imaging

red_flags.finding: Midline cervical tenderness or a distracting injury
red_flags.meaning: Possible cervical spine injury; immobilize and image before clearing the neck
Associated multisystem trauma or shock; resuscitate before imaging

complications.name: Epidural hematoma
clues: Temporal blow with a brief loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval
Rapidly worsening headache and drowsiness
Lens-shaped hyperdense collection on CT

complications.name: Acute subdural hematoma
clues: Older adult or anticoagulated patient
Progressive confusion and focal deficit
Crescent-shaped hyperdense collection on CT

complications.name: Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage
clues: Severe headache and neck stiffness after trauma
Blood in the sulci or cisterns on CT

complications.name: Cerebral contusion with edema
clues: Frontal or temporal impact
Persistent confusion or focal deficit
Mixed-density lesion with surrounding edema on CT

complications.name: Diffuse axonal injury
clues: High-speed deceleration mechanism
Prolonged coma out of proportion to CT findings
Punctate white matter lesions on MRI

complications.name: Raised intracranial pressure and herniation
clues: Declining Glasgow Coma Scale
Pupillary asymmetry
Cushing response with hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respirations

complications.name: Post-traumatic seizure
clues: Seizure within the first week after injury
Cortical contusion, hemorrhage or depressed fracture on imaging

complications.name: Cerebrospinal fluid leak and meningitis
clues: Clear fluid from the nose or ear
Basilar skull fracture on imaging
Fever and neck stiffness days later

complications.name: Chronic subdural hematoma
clues: Older adult with weeks of headache, gait change or confusion
Minor or forgotten head injury
Hypodense or mixed-density crescentic collection on CT

complications.name: Post-concussion syndrome
clues: Headache, dizziness, poor concentration and irritability lasting weeks
Symptoms provoked by exertion, screens or noise

complications.name: Cognitive and neuroendocrine sequelae
clues: Persistent memory or executive dysfunction
Fatigue, weight change or hypotension suggesting hypopituitarism

special_populations.differences: Infants and young children may present with irritability, poor feeding, vomiting or a bulging fontanelle rather than reporting headache or confusion. Non-accidental trauma should be considered when the mechanism does not fit the injury, and the PECARN rule guides imaging.

Even a minor fall can cause a subdural hematoma, and symptoms may be subtle: new confusion, gait change or drowsiness rather than a dramatic headache. Anticoagulant use raises the risk substantially, and a lower threshold for CT and repeat imaging is warranted.

Trauma evaluation must also consider the pregnancy; imaging decisions balance fetal radiation exposure against the need to exclude intracranial bleeding. Symptoms of head injury can be confused with preeclampsia or eclampsia.
A minor head injury can be more serious because of bleeding risk from low platelets or coagulopathy; infection of a scalp wound or skull fracture is also more likely.

key_questions.question: What happened, and how did you hit your head?
key_questions.looking_for: A clear mechanism (fall, crash, assault, sports collision) and the height or force involved; a dangerous mechanism such as a fall from more than 3 feet or 5 stairs, ejection from a vehicle, or a pedestrian struck raises the risk of intracranial injury

key_questions.question: Did you lose consciousness, and if so, for how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Any loss of consciousness, however brief; a lucid interval followed by worsening drowsiness suggests an expanding epidural hematoma

key_questions.question: Do you remember what happened right before and right after the injury?
key_questions.looking_for: Amnesia around the event; amnesia longer than 30 minutes before impact is a medium-risk feature on the Canadian CT Head Rule

key_questions.question: Is your headache getting worse, and have you vomited?
key_questions.looking_for: Worsening or persistent headache and repeated vomiting, which suggest rising intracranial pressure or an expanding hematoma

key_questions.question: Have you felt drowsier, harder to wake, or more confused since the injury?
key_questions.looking_for: Progressive decline in level of consciousness, which is the most important warning sign of a worsening intracranial injury

key_questions.question: Any weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or trouble seeing?
key_questions.looking_for: New focal deficits such as limb weakness, slurred speech, or visual change, which point to intracranial hemorrhage, contusion, or mass effect

key_questions.question: Did you have a seizure after the injury?
key_questions.looking_for: A post-traumatic seizure, which indicates cortical irritation and warrants imaging and monitoring

key_questions.question: Any clear fluid or blood dripping from your nose or ear?
key_questions.looking_for: CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea, raccoon eyes, or Battle sign, which suggest a basilar skull fracture

key_questions.question: Does your neck hurt, especially in the middle?
key_questions.looking_for: Midline cervical tenderness, which raises concern for a cervical spine injury and requires immobilization and imaging

key_questions.question: Do you take any blood thinners, such as warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, aspirin, or clopidogrel?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, which markedly raises the risk of delayed intracranial hemorrhage and lowers the threshold for CT and repeat imaging

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a head injury or brain surgery before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior head injury or neurosurgery, which increases vulnerability to a new injury and can complicate interpretation of imaging

key_questions.question: Do you have a bleeding disorder, liver disease, or a low platelet count?
key_questions.looking_for: A coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia, which raises bleeding risk and may require reversal or transfusion before neurosurgery

key_questions.question: Had you been drinking alcohol or using any drugs before the injury?
key_questions.looking_for: Alcohol or drug use, which can cause the fall and also confound the neurologic exam; intoxication is a risk feature on the New Orleans Criteria

key_questions.question: Were you wearing a helmet or seatbelt?
key_questions.looking_for: Absence of protective equipment, which supports a higher-energy mechanism and a lower threshold for imaging

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Possible pregnancy, which must be excluded before CT imaging and changes the imaging and management plan

key_questions.question: Do you have any other injuries, such as chest, abdominal, or limb pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Associated multisystem trauma, which may be more immediately life-threatening than the head injury and changes resuscitation priorities

reasoning_points: A clear mechanism of trauma to the head, such as a fall, motor vehicle crash, assault, or sports collision
Headache, confusion or feeling foggy, dizziness, and nausea after the impact
Amnesia around the event or a brief loss of consciousness
Glasgow Coma Scale below 15 or an altered level of consciousness on exam
Focal neurologic deficits, pupillary asymmetry, or signs of raised intracranial pressure
External signs of trauma such as a scalp laceration, hematoma, raccoon eyes, Battle sign, or hemotympanum
Risk factors that lower the threshold for imaging: age 65 or older, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, vomiting, dangerous mechanism, or post-traumatic seizure
Noncontrast CT head showing hemorrhage, contusion, mass effect, or skull fracture, or a normal study in concussion
Reversible causes of altered mental status such as hypoglycemia and intoxication excluded
Cervical spine injury considered and the neck cleared or imaged before mobilization

easy: Young adult with a clear blow to the head after a fall or collision
Headache, dizziness, and nausea with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15
Scalp laceration or hematoma at the site of impact
No focal deficit and a normal noncontrast CT head
medium: Older adult on warfarin or an antiplatelet agent after a ground-level fall
Brief loss of consciousness with a lucid interval followed by worsening drowsiness
Post-traumatic seizure with a cortical contusion on CT
Basilar skull fracture signs such as raccoon eyes, Battle sign, or clear fluid from the ear
hard: Patient with alcohol intoxication whose confusion is attributed to drinking rather than the head injury
Older adult with weeks of subtle confusion or gait change from a chronic subdural hematoma and a forgotten fall
High-speed deceleration injury with prolonged coma out of proportion to a near-normal CT (diffuse axonal injury)
Patient with a focal deficit from a stroke who fell afterward, so the trauma is mistaken for the cause
Toddler with irritability and vomiting where non-accidental trauma must be considered
